question: For take-off planning, when is a runway contaminated?

options.text: When it is damp over its whole length
When more than 10% is covered by water of any depth
When any part of it is wet
Over 25% covered by more than 3 mm of water or equivalent

explanation: The test is more than 25% of the surface area (within the length and width used), whether in patches or not, covered by water over 3 mm deep or by slush or loose snow equivalent to more than 3 mm of water.

question: Why does slush or standing water increase the take-off distance required?

options.text: It reduces the engine thrust
It adds wheel and spray drag
It reduces the stall speed
It increases the lift on the main wheels during the ground run

explanation: Displacement drag on the gear and spray impingement drag reduce acceleration, so more distance is needed to reach the take-off speeds.

question: Why does contamination increase the accelerate-stop distance required?

options.text: Slower acceleration, poor braking
It increases the reverse thrust available
It reduces V1
It increases the brake energy limit and the stopping distance with it

explanation: The aeroplane takes longer to reach V1, and then the reduced friction makes the stop much longer.

question: Compared with a dry runway, what happens to the maximum take-off mass and V1 on a contaminated runway?

options.text: They are unchanged if anti-skid works
Both are increased
Both are reduced
The mass is reduced; V1 is increased

explanation: For the same distances available, both the maximum take-off mass and V1 are reduced.

question: As the depth of contamination increases, how do the corrections change?

options.text: Both reductions get smaller
A smaller mass reduction and a larger V1 reduction
Both reductions get larger
A larger mass reduction and a smaller V1 reduction

explanation: Deeper contaminant needs a greater mass reduction, but the V1 reduction is less.

question: Which drag change is allowed for in the acceleration on a contaminated runway above the aquaplaning speed?

options.text: Contaminant drag doubles
Contaminant drag is unchanged
Contaminant drag decreases
Aerodynamic drag disappears

explanation: Contaminant drag rises with speed up to the aquaplaning speed, then decreases as the tyres ride on the surface.

question: What is the first step in finding the take-off mass for a contaminated runway?

options.text: Find the dry runway limiting mass
Find the landing mass at the destination
Set V1 equal to VMCG
Find the mass limited only by the tyre speed on a wet runway

explanation: The dry runway limiting mass (field, climb or obstacle) is found first; the contaminant table then gives a mass reduction from it.

question: In the contaminated runway procedure, what does the shaded area of the table mean?

options.text: The V1 reduction is doubled
Also find a TORA mass, V1 = VMCG
No mass reduction is needed
The take-off is always prohibited in those conditions

explanation: If the result is in the shaded area, a second table gives a maximum mass from the TORA with V1 set to VMCG; the lower of the two masses is used.

question: After the contaminated runway V1 reduction, the adjusted V1 is below VMCG. What does this mean?

options.text: The reduction is ignored
V1 is set equal to VR
Take-off is not permitted
The flap setting is reduced

explanation: V1 may never be less than VMCG; if the adjusted V1 falls below it, take-off is not permitted.

question: From what height does the take-off climb start after a take-off from a contaminated runway?

options.text: 400 ft
15 ft
35 ft
50 ft

explanation: With a contaminated runway the take-off flight path begins at 15 ft rather than 35 ft.

question: When is the increased V2 (improved climb) procedure used?

options.text: When the runway is contaminated
When the runway is too short for a normal take-off at the planned mass
When an engine has already failed
Climb-limited, with spare runway

explanation: If the climb limit gives a much lower mass than the field limit, the spare runway can be used to accelerate to a higher V2.

question: Why does a higher V2 improve the climb gradient?

options.text: V2 is normally well below VX, so a faster speed gives more excess thrust
A faster speed reduces the weight
A faster speed allows less flap
A faster speed reduces the parasite drag of the gear and flaps

explanation: V2 is considerably slower than the best angle of climb speed. Raising it towards VX increases excess thrust and the gradient, raising the climb-limited mass.

question: The field limit mass is 61 000 kg and the climb limit mass 52 000 kg. What does the improved climb procedure do?

options.text: It reduces V2 so less runway is used
It raises the climb limit using spare runway
It increases the climb limit mass above the field limit mass
It reduces the field limit mass to 52 000 kg

explanation: Staying on the runway longer gives higher speeds at rotation and at the screen, so the climb limit mass rises, though not beyond what the field and tyre limits allow.

question: In the improved climb procedure, which two limits are compared with the climb limit mass?

options.text: The obstacle limit and the landing limit
The brake energy limit and the zero fuel limit
The landing limit and the structural limit
The field limit and the tyre speed limit

explanation: The mass improvement is read from charts using (field limit − climb limit) and (tyre limit − climb limit); the lower improvement, with its speed increments, is used.

question: After applying the improved climb speed increments, which speed must be checked?

options.text: VMCL
VMO
VMBE
VREF

explanation: The higher V1 must still not exceed the brake energy limit, so VMBE is checked last.

question: Why is a reduced thrust (assumed temperature) take-off used?

options.text: For engine life and less noise
To allow a higher take-off mass
To increase the climb gradient
To shorten the take-off distance on long runways

explanation: When the actual mass is below the maximum and the runway is long enough, using less than full thrust preserves engine life and reduces noise.

question: What is the greatest reduction from full rated take-off thrust normally allowed for a reduced thrust take-off?
explanation: The maximum reduction from full rated take-off thrust is 25%.

question: How does the assumed temperature method work?

options.text: Thrust is set for a temperature colder than the actual one at the airport
The flaps are set for a higher temperature
Thrust is set for a hotter temperature
The engines are run at idle until V1

explanation: The thrust is set as if the air were hotter, at the highest temperature at which the take-off could still meet all requirements at the actual mass.

question: In which case is a reduced thrust take-off NOT permitted?

options.text: With the actual mass well below the maximum
With anti-skid inoperative
With a long runway
With a dry runway

explanation: Reduced thrust is not permitted on icy, very slippery or contaminated runways, with anti-skid or reverse inoperative, with the increased V2 procedure, or with the power management control off.

question: Which runway condition prohibits a reduced thrust take-off?

options.text: A displaced threshold
A dry grooved surface
A 1% upslope
Contamination

explanation: Reduced thrust is not permitted on contaminated, icy or very slippery runways.

question: In which weather is a reduced thrust take-off not recommended?

options.text: In a steady crosswind within limits
In light rain on a dry runway
At night
When windshear may be present

explanation: Reduced thrust is not recommended if potential windshear conditions exist, when full thrust may be needed quickly.

question: How is the assumed temperature chosen?

options.text: The highest of the maximum temperatures allowed by any of the limits
The ISA temperature for the aerodrome
The lowest of the maximum temperatures allowed by each performance limit
The actual temperature plus 25°C

explanation: For the actual mass, the maximum permissible temperature is found from the field, climb, tyre and obstacle limits; the lowest is used, within the maximum and minimum assumed temperature limits.

question: Which further limits apply to the assumed temperature?

options.text: It must lie between set limits
It must be at least 25°C above the actual outside air temperature
It must not exceed ISA
It must equal the flat rating temperature

explanation: The assumed temperature may not exceed the maximum allowed for the ambient temperature and altitude, and may not be below the minimum assumed temperature.

question: What is a derated take-off?

options.text: A take-off with reduced flap
A fixed thrust reduction with its own data
A take-off at an assumed temperature
A take-off with one engine at idle

explanation: Derate gives a fixed thrust reduction (for example a few percent or 10%) treated as a separate rating with its own performance data.

question: Why can derated thrust allow a higher take-off mass on a short runway?

options.text: Derated thrust increases the climb gradient
Derated thrust shortens the stopping distance
Derated thrust gives more acceleration
VMCG and VMCA are lower at the derated thrust

explanation: Minimum control speeds depend on the thrust, so a fixed lower thrust gives lower VMCG and VMCA, which can relieve a VMCG-limited V1.

question: What is a key difference between assumed temperature and derated thrust in an emergency?

options.text: With assumed temperature, thrust may never be increased after brake release
Derate: do not add thrust near VMC
With derate, full thrust is always safe at any speed
There is no difference

explanation: With an assumed temperature, full thrust remains available. With derate, the speeds are based on the lower thrust, so raising thrust near the minimum control speed could cause loss of control.

question: Why does an inoperative anti-skid system affect the take-off?

options.text: The accelerate-stop distance increases greatly
The climb gradient falls
The tyre speed limit falls
The take-off distance increases greatly on dry runways

explanation: Without anti-skid the stopping ability is much reduced, so the accelerate-stop distance required rises sharply.

question: With anti-skid inoperative, what is done to V1 and the take-off mass?

options.text: V1 is reduced; mass is increased
Both are increased
Both are reduced
V1 is increased; mass is reduced

explanation: Reducing V1 shortens the ASDR but lengthens the TODR, so the mass must also be reduced to keep both within the field.
